clinicalPearls: VZV causes two distinct clinical syndromes: primary infection (varicella/chickenpox), usually a benign childhood exanthematous vesicular illness, and reactivation of latent virus (herpes zoster/shingles), a dermatomal vesicular rash usually associated with severe pain (p.1504).

In chickenpox, skin lesions appear in successive crops over a 2-4 day period and are present in various stages of evolution simultaneously (maculopapules, vesicles, and scabs) on a given body region - the classic small vesicle on an erythematous base ('dewdrop on a rose petal') (p.1505).

Chickenpox is highly contagious (attack rate >=90% in seronegatives); patients are infectious ~48 h before the rash appears, throughout vesicle formation, and until all vesicles are crusted. Incubation is usually 14-17 days (range 10-21) (p.1505).

Herpes zoster results from reactivation of latent VZV in dorsal root ganglia; most patients have no recent exposure to others with VZV. Incidence is highest in the sixth decade of life and beyond; recurrent zoster is exceedingly rare except in immunocompromised hosts, especially those with AIDS (p.1505).
Zoster pain (dermatomal) may precede visible lesions by 48-72 h; in the prodromal stage before the rash appears, the diagnosis can be exceedingly difficult (p.1505-1506).
Dermatomes T3 to L3 are most frequently involved in herpes zoster (p.1505).

PCR detection of VZV DNA in vesicular fluid is the diagnostic method of choice; specimens for PCR include lesions, blood, and saliva. The Tzanck smear gives a rapid impression but has low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507).
Patients with herpes zoster can transmit infection to seronegative individuals, resulting in chickenpox (not zoster) in the contact (p.1506).
harrison.pathophysiology: VZV is a member of the Herpesviridae with double-stranded DNA (~125,000 bp), a lipid envelope, and an icosahedral nucleocapsid (~180-200 nm). Primary transmission is by the respiratory route, with localized replication (presumably nasopharynx) seeding the lymphatic/reticuloendothelial system and producing viremia, which manifests as diffuse, scattered skin lesions. Vesicles involve the corium/dermis with ballooning degeneration, multinucleated giant cells, and eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions; localized skin blood-vessel involvement can cause necrosis and epidermal hemorrhage. During chickenpox the virus infects dorsal root ganglia and remains latent (in sensory dorsal, cranial, and enteric ganglia) until an unknown trigger causes reactivation, producing herpes zoster; active zoster ganglia show hemorrhage, edema, and lymphocytic infiltration. Pulmonary involvement shows interstitial pneumonitis with giant cells, intranuclear inclusions, and hemorrhage; CNS infection produces perivascular cuffing similar to other viral encephalitides, while focal hemorrhagic necrosis (characteristic of HSV encephalitis) develops infrequently in VZV infection (p.1504).
additionalDifferentials: For chickenpox: disseminated HSV infection in patients with atopic dermatitis; disseminated vesiculopapular lesions of coxsackievirus or echovirus infection; atypical measles (these rashes are more often morbilliform/hemorrhagic than vesicular) (p.1506)
Rickettsialpox - distinguished by the 'herald spot' (eschar) at the mite-bite site and a more pronounced headache; serology helps differentiate it from varicella (p.1506)
Mpox - consider in travelers from endemic areas and in HIV-infected individuals (p.1506)
Smallpox - bioterrorism concern; smallpox lesions are larger than chickenpox lesions and all at the same stage of evolution at any given time (p.1506)
For herpes zoster: both HSV and coxsackievirus infections can cause dermatomal vesicular lesions (p.1506)
infectionMimics: Disseminated HSV infection (notably in atopic dermatitis) (p.1506)
HSV and coxsackievirus causing dermatomal vesicular lesions (mimicking zoster) (p.1506)
additionalInvestigations: PCR for VZV DNA in vesicular fluid - diagnostic method of choice; also performed on lesions, blood, and saliva (p.1507)
Tzanck smear (scraping of lesion base for multinucleated giant cells) - rapid but low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507)
Viral isolation in susceptible tissue-culture cell lines (unequivocal confirmation) (p.1507)
Direct immunofluorescent staining of cells from the lesion base or immunoperoxidase detection of viral antigens (p.1507)

Serology: seroconversion or fourfold rise in antibody titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera; FAMA (fluorescent antibody to membrane antigen) test and ELISA are the most sensitive serologic tools (p.1507)
redFlags: Zoster ophthalmicus - involvement of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve; a debilitating condition that can result in blindness in the absence of antiviral therapy. Lesions on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) signal likely ocular involvement; refer immediately to an ophthalmologist (p.1505-1507)

Ramsay Hunt syndrome - geniculate ganglion (sensory branch of facial nerve) involvement causing pain and vesicles in the external auditory canal, loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and ipsilateral facial palsy (p.1506)

Disseminated/progressive herpes zoster in immunocompromised hosts - patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma are at greatest risk; cutaneous dissemination occurs in ~40% untreated, raising the risk of pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis, and hepatitis by 5-10% (p.1506)

Varicella pneumonia - the most serious complication of chickenpox; more common in adults (up to 20%) than children and particularly severe in pregnant women; typically requires ventilatory support (p.1505, 1507)
Visceral dissemination in immunocompromised patients - occurs in 30-50% of cases and is fatal 15% of the time without antiviral therapy (p.1505)
Perinatal varicella - mortality as high as 30% when maternal disease begins within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1505)

CNS involvement: encephalitis (0.1-0.2% of children with chickenpox), aseptic meningitis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome; in zoster, symptomatic meningoencephalitis and rare granulomatous angiitis with contralateral hemiplegia (p.1505-1506)
harrison.prognosis: In the immunocompetent host chickenpox is usually benign and self-limited (total duration ~7-10 days; skin may take 2-4 weeks to fully normalize). Childhood acute cerebellar ataxia is generally benign and does not require hospitalization. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most debilitating complication of zoster: uncommon in the young but affects at least 50% of patients over age 50, who report dermatomal pain for months after cutaneous healing. Even in immunocompromised patients, disseminated zoster is rarely fatal. Hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients are at particularly high risk, with a mortality rate of ~10% for posttransplantation VZV infection. The Shingrix subunit vaccine showed 97.2% efficacy in adults >=50 years, although vaccine immunity wanes over time (p.1505-1507).
pitfalls: Aspirin should never be given to children with chickenpox because of its association with Reye syndrome; aspirin is no longer used for this reason (p.1505, 1507)
Zoster sine herpetica: dermatomal pain with serologic evidence of zoster can occur in the absence of any skin lesions - shingles without a rash has been reported, making diagnosis difficult (p.1506)
In the prodromal stage of herpes zoster (before lesions appear), diagnosis may be possible only after lesions emerge or by retrospective serology (p.1506)

Glucocorticoids for zoster should not be used without concomitant antiviral therapy, and steroid use is appropriate only for relatively healthy elderly patients with moderate/severe pain; patients with osteoporosis, diabetes mellitus, glycosuria, or hypertension may not be appropriate candidates (p.1507)
VZIG is NOT indicated for a newborn if the mother has zoster (as opposed to varicella); it is indicated when maternal varicella onsets within 5 days before to 48 h after delivery (p.1507-1508)

management: Antiviral therapy with aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir, most beneficial when started early, for herpes zoster and for varicella in adolescents, adults and the immunocompromised or complicated cases
Intravenous aciclovir for severe or disseminated disease and immunocompromised hosts
Symptomatic care of varicella with antipyretics such as paracetamol, avoiding aspirin because of Reye syndrome, plus antipruritics and skin hygiene to prevent secondary bacterial infection
Analgesia for zoster and multimodal management of postherpetic neuralgia with agents such as tricyclic antidepressants, gabapentinoids and topical lidocaine or capsaicin
Urgent ophthalmology referral for herpes zoster ophthalmicus and specialist input for other complications
Infection control with respiratory and contact isolation until lesions crust, and post-exposure prophylaxis with varicella-zoster immunoglobulin or vaccine for susceptible high-risk contacts
Prevention through varicella vaccination and recombinant zoster vaccination in eligible groups
